summary: Gives scenarios that illustrate what happens when two content networks decide to interconnect, to make the idea of content internetworking concrete. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 6770.

eli5.summary: Two networks that deliver websites faster could join up. This memo tells a few little stories about what that would look like step by step.

questions: what is a content delivery network
subtitle: How content networks interconnect to serve users faster and more reliably

tldr.problem: Content networks exist to serve websites and media faster, but they operate independently. When they want to interconnect to expand their reach, the arrangements involve complex coordination of request routing, content distribution, and billing.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3570 presents five detailed scenarios showing how content networks establish negotiated relationships, configure their interconnection gateways, and coordinate the distribution of content to surrogates and routing of client requests.
tldr.outcome: The scenarios demonstrate that content internetworking requires three coordinated systems: request-routing (directing clients to the best server), distribution (copying content to edge servers), and accounting (tracking usage). It was replaced by RFC 6770.

today: RFC 3570 is Informational and was replaced by RFC 6770. However, the concepts of content networks, surrogates, and the three core internetworking systems remain relevant to understanding modern content delivery infrastructure.

sections.title: Content Internetworking Scenarios
sections.content:
A content network is a system that stores copies of websites and media on servers distributed across the Internet to serve users faster. Content internetworking occurs when two or more separate content networks decide to interconnect to expand their scale and reach.

RFC 3570 provides concrete scenarios that illustrate what happens when content networks interconnect. The scenarios are designed both to help people understand what content internetworking is and to provide a basis for evaluating proposals. The document assumes that readers are familiar with the basic concepts from RFC 3466, which defines the content internetworking model including CONTENT NETWORKS (CNs), SURROGATES (caching servers), PUBLISHERs (content originators), and CLIENTS (end users).
sections.eli5: Content networks store popular websites on servers near users so pages load faster. This document shows examples of how two networks could work together to cover more of the world.

sections.title: Types of Content Networks
sections.content:
RFC 3570 describes three specialized types of content networks designed to participate in content internetworking.

A Publishing Content Network (PCN) is maintained by a publisher and contains the authoritative system for directing client requests. A PCN may contain surrogates to serve its own content locally but does not serve content on behalf of other publishers. The PCN participates in all three content internetworking interfaces (request-routing, distribution, and accounting) with other networks.

A Brokering Content Network (BCN) does not operate its own surrogates; instead, it acts as a clearinghouse that aggregates information and services on behalf of other networks. A BCN might aggregate distribution advertisements from multiple networks or combine accounting data from several sources. It participates only in the interfaces needed for these brokering services.

A Local Request-Routing Content Network (LCN) serves all client requests locally (for example, through a corporate caching proxy). Clients' requests are always handled by a local server within the same administrative domain. Because of this local handling, LCNs only send distribution advertisements and accounting data; they do not participate in request-routing internetworking with other networks.
sections.eli5: There are three types of networks: ones that own content (PCN), ones that just aggregate information (BCN), and ones that only serve their own users locally (LCN).

sections.title: Setting Up Interconnection Relationships
sections.content:
When two content networks decide to interconnect, multiple steps occur.

First, the controlling organizations create a negotiated relationship—typically a legal document describing the services to be provided, costs, service level agreements (SLAs), and other business terms. For example, a network might agree to distribute content into a particular geographic region or maintain certain performance levels.

Second, the networks configure Content Internetworking Gateways (CIGs) on their respective networks. CIGs are the systems through which the three content internetworking functions are implemented: REQUEST-ROUTING INTERNETWORKING (agreeing on which surrogate should serve a client), DISTRIBUTION INTERNETWORKING (distributing content to surrogates), and ACCOUNTING INTERNETWORKING (sharing usage data).

Technical details such as gateway addresses and authentication information are exchanged. The negotiated relationship may include non-technical terms (like payment) that are handled outside the scope of the internetworking protocols.

When networks wish to disconnect, the configurations are reversed: the protocol connections are shut down and the negotiated relationship is legally terminated.
sections.eli5: Two networks make a deal about what they'll do together. Then they set up computers to talk to each other and exchange content and usage information.

sections.title: Content Internetworking Scenarios
sections.content:
RFC 3570 provides five detailed scenarios showing different configurations of content networks and how they interact.

General Content Internetworking shows three or more networks of equal capability interconnecting via content internetworking gateways. All participate in distribution, request-routing, and accounting. Content injected into any network can be distributed to others, and all networks share accounting information.

BCN providing Accounting and Request-Routing describes a brokering network that handles accounting data from multiple content networks and provides a unified request-routing service, but does not handle distribution. This works as a clearinghouse for settlements and routing decisions.

BCN providing Accounting Only shows a broker that aggregates accounting information without participating in request-routing or distribution, while the content networks handle distribution and routing independently.

PCN Enlisting Multiple Networks describes a publisher that maintains its own authoritative request-routing system and directly negotiates with multiple content networks to distribute its content and collect accounting data.

Multiple Networks Enlisting an LCN shows multiple content networks distributing content to a local request-routing network (such as a corporate proxy) that serves all requests locally. The networks send distribution advertisements but do not participate in request-routing decisions.
sections.eli5: These five examples show different ways networks could team up: some networks doing everything together, some networks using a broker, some publishers controlling the routing themselves, or networks feeding a local proxy.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Content internetworking introduces several security risks because surrogates may be located in different jurisdictions, operated by different companies, or have less robust security than origin servers.

Threats to Clients include defeat of client security settings (a surrogate location may bypass client protections), bad accounting information (charges for content not received), bad content delivery (wrong or misleading content), denial of service (no access to content), exposure of private information (passwords, browsing patterns), and substitution of security parameters or policies (surrogates with weaker encryption or different security procedures).

Threats to Publishers include bad accounting information (inability to charge clients), denial of service, and substitution of security parameters or policies. If a surrogate in a different jurisdiction has different legal requirements, the publisher's content may not be as secure as expected.

Threats to Content Networks include bad accounting information (inability to collect payment), denial of service attacks on the accounting, distribution, or request-routing systems, and transitive threats (when networks act as both clients and publishers in complex arrangements).

The RFC notes that content internetworking systems rely on a trust model where all participating systems (origins, gateways, surrogates) are considered "insiders" and are therefore trusted. This assumes proper configuration and honest operation of all parties.
sections.eli5: When content goes through extra servers, there are risks: clients might be charged wrongly, wrong content could be delivered, security could be weaker, and data could leak.
